title: Close the old customer version before opening the new one
goal: Preserve one non-overlapping Type-2 history when customer changes arrive late or are replayed.
tag: Certification cycle 1 · focused lesson 5 · CDC transformation and history
concept:
A passport office does not erase your old passport when it issues a new one. It stamps the old validity period closed and opens a new period.

A slowly changing dimension Type 2 table does the same for business facts. Each key has dated versions. A change for customer c56 at time 20 closes the current basic row at 20 and inserts pro starting at 20. The hard invariant is not “keep two rows”; it is “for one key, validity ranges do not overlap and one row is current.” Sequence evidence, duplicate handling, deletes, null rules, and late events must be explicit.
example: Before: c56 | basic | [0,∞). After the event (c56, pro, ts=20): basic | [0,20) and pro | [20,∞). Replaying the exact event must not create a second pro row.

use_case.when: Use Type-2 history when analytics or audit questions need the value that was valid at an earlier business time.
use_case.example: A financial data platform must explain which customer tier and risk segment applied when an order was approved.
use_case.decision: Choose Type 2 only for attributes whose history matters. Use Type 1 for corrections where old values have no business meaning. Define sequence, tie, delete, late-arrival, and replay rules before choosing a product mechanism.

practice: Apply the c56 event, then replay it. Predict the row ranges and current-row count.
boundary: The local worlds model one key and one ordered update. They do not run Lakeflow AUTO CDC, Delta, Snowflake streams/tasks, transactions, late events, deletes, schema evolution, bitemporal history, concurrent writers, retention, or production recovery.

product_sections.title: Snowflake: make close-and-insert an explicit stream/task transaction
product_sections.html:
First-minute product recall: Recall Day31: a Snowflake stream exposes a change interval and advances when committed DML consumes it.

-- Snowflake SQL sketch; not executedBEGIN;UPDATE dim_customer d SET valid_to=s.event_ts, is_current=FALSE  FROM customer_stream s  WHERE d.customer_id=s.customer_id AND d.is_current;INSERT INTO dim_customer  SELECT customer_id,tier,event_ts,NULL,TRUE FROM customer_stream;COMMIT;

A stream plus triggered task can drive explicit change processing. Snowflake MERGE is useful, but Type 2 needs both closing the old row and inserting a new row; many designs stage action rows or use a stored procedure/explicit transaction. Deduplicate the source first because multiple source rows matching one target can make MERGE nondeterministic. This is not a direct managed equivalent of AUTO CDC.

Execution label. SQL was not run in Snowflake; this is a local JavaScript teaching model.
product_sections.markdown: Recall Day31's stream offset boundary. Snowflake stream/task processing makes Type-2 close-and-insert explicit; keep both effects in a transaction and deduplicate before MERGE. There is no direct managed AUTO CDC equivalent. SQL not executed in Snowflake.

title: invokeAny returns the first success—not the first task to finish
goal: Race equivalent providers without letting an early failure hide a later successful answer.
concept:
Three couriers race to deliver the same parcel. The first courier may call to say the van broke down. That is not the first delivery.

ExecutorService.invokeAny runs a collection of callables and returns one result that completed successfully. An early exception does not win. If none succeeds, it throws ExecutionException; the timed overload can throw TimeoutException. On return, unfinished tasks are cancelled, but cancellation is an attempt—not proof that external work stopped.
example: Replica A fails at 10 ms. Replica B returns order-56 at 30 ms. Replica C is still running. invokeAny returns B’s value and cancels C. A custom “first completion” race would incorrectly surface A’s failure.

use_case.when: Use invokeAny when several equivalent computations or replicas may produce one acceptable answer and first success is the contract.
use_case.example: A Java service races two read replicas for the same immutable catalog record during a regional degradation.
use_case.decision: Use it only for equivalent, safe-to-duplicate operations. Keep a shared deadline, make losers cancellation-aware, and do not race side effects such as payments. Use CompletionService when you need custom acceptance or evidence from multiple results.

practice: Change the first completion from failure to success. Predict the returned value and loser state.
boundary: The Java and browser models use a scripted completion order. They do not create real threads, model scheduling, network calls, interrupt handling, timeout clocks, executor saturation, or guarantee cancellation of external effects.

title: A healthy global average can hide one tenant in pain
goal: Make platform reliability decisions from tenant and tier distributions, not only aggregate success.
concept:
If nine checkout lanes are empty and one has a hundred people, the store’s average queue can still look small. The people in the bad lane do not experience the average.

A shared platform can report 99.9% overall success while a small tenant repeatedly fails. Distinguished-level judgment keeps the global SLO but adds tenant/tier views, minimum-volume rules, top-offender evidence, and a response policy. Do not create thousands of noisy pages; use distributions and drill-downs to find concentrated harm.
example: Tenant A sends 999,000 successful requests. Tenant B sends 1,000 requests and 500 fail. Global success is about 99.95%; B experiences only 50%. The platform is globally green and locally broken.

use_case.when: Use tenant-aware reliability views when a shared service has uneven traffic and aggregate metrics can be dominated by large users.
use_case.example: A data-quality API serves forty producer teams; one smaller team cannot register rules although the fleet dashboard is green.
use_case.decision: Retain a global objective for capacity and business health, then add tier and tenant distributions with minimum-volume confidence rules. Page on actionable widespread harm; route concentrated degradation to an owned incident or ticket policy.

practice: Move failed requests between the large and small tenant. Predict global and tenant success.
boundary: The model has two tenants and a single success metric. It does not handle sampling confidence, latency, retries, traffic weighting, tier contracts, low-volume burn rates, regional cells, alert routing, or privacy limits.

title: A task ID may be a bearer secret—authorize every poll
goal: Keep durable MCP task state bound to the original caller across disconnects and follow-up requests.
tag: GenAI engineering · harness security · MCP Tasks extension
concept:
A coat-check ticket is useful because it retrieves something later. If anyone holding the number can claim the coat, the number is also a secret.

The MCP Tasks extension allows a task ID to identify durable stored state, and the specification says it may act as a bearer token. IDs must be hard to guess, but entropy is not authorization. Every tasks/get, tasks/update, and tasks/cancel request must authenticate and authorize the caller. A client that resumes by ID must carry the original request context—headers, tenant, and timeout policy—into follow-ups.
example: Tenant red starts task t56. Tenant blue learns the ID from a log. A server that checks only “does t56 exist?” leaks status and perhaps results. A safe lookup checks task.owner == caller.tenant before returning anything.

use_case.when: Use durable tasks for expensive MCP tool work that must survive disconnects or require later input.
use_case.example: A lineage extraction tool returns a task handle while a Spark plan is analyzed asynchronously.
use_case.decision: Use opaque high-entropy IDs, bind stored tasks to authenticated principal and authorization policy, propagate wire context to every follow-up, redact IDs from logs, expire state, and avoid tasks when synchronous work is short enough.

practice: Switch the polling tenant from red to blue. Predict whether task status is returned.
boundary: The model compares two tenant strings. It does not implement MCP transport, token validation, capability negotiation, cryptographic entropy, task storage, expiry, cancellation, input requests, log redaction, or cross-region recovery.

title: One membrane can open from nanometres to submillimetres—but the control spans five orders of magnitude
goal: Read a newly reported tunable membrane as a reversible spacing mechanism, not a ready universal filter.
tag: Technology breakthroughs · new peer-reviewed research · November 16, 2026
concept:
A book can be tightly closed or fanned open. The same pages create very different gaps without changing the page material.

A Nature Materials paper reports layered membranes whose interlayer spacing is reversibly controlled by deprotonation-driven electrostatic repulsion and cation coordination. Reported spacing spans 1.39 to 152,000 nm, porosity 0% to 78%, and thickness 43 to 5,400 μm. Demonstrations tune zinc-ion capacitance, osmotic power, and pressure sensing. Those outcomes occur at very different openings; “bigger gap” is not one universal optimum.
example: Our visual places 1.39 nm, 140 nm, and 140,000 nm on a logarithmic scale. On a linear bar, the first two would look identical. The log view makes the five-order range visible without pretending that spacing alone predicts performance.

use_case.when: Study the strategy when a materials team needs one membrane platform with reversibly adjustable transport or sensing geometry.
use_case.example: A lab explores whether ion coordination can retune a layered membrane between ion storage, osmotic conversion, and pressure-sensing regimes.
use_case.decision: Treat the publication as a mechanism and materials platform. Reproduce cycling, selectivity, response time, chemical stability, mechanical fatigue, scale-up, and the target device metric before choosing it over a fixed membrane.

practice: Choose three reported-scale gaps and compare them on linear versus logarithmic axes.
boundary: The local model plots spacing only. It does not simulate charge, cation coordination, porosity, thickness coupling, ion transport, capacitance, osmotic conversion, pressure response, cycling, fabrication, or reproduce the paper's datasets.

title: A readable action tag can move; the lockfile chooses the commit that runs
goal: Keep review-friendly GitHub Actions references while executing the exact reviewed dependency commits.
concept:
A restaurant menu can keep the friendly name “house soup,” but the kitchen needs the exact recipe version approved for today.

GitHub Actions workflow dependency lockfiles, generally available on October 28, 2026, let workflow YAML retain readable tag or branch references while the runner executes recorded commits. Onboarded workflows require dependencies in .github/workflows/actions.lock. Dependabot can update the reference and lock entry together. The lockfile reduces unexpected movement; it does not prove the locked code is safe.
example: The workflow says uses: vendor/scan@v3. Yesterday the lock maps it to commit abc56. The tag later moves to bad99. With a current enforced lock, the run still executes abc56; without it, the tag resolves to the moved code.

use_case.when: Use workflow lockfiles when many actions and transitive dependencies make manual SHA pinning hard to review and maintain.
use_case.example: An enterprise data-platform repository runs third-party build, scan, and cloud-auth actions before production deployment.
use_case.decision: Review dependencies before locking, enforce lockfiles in stages, verify staleness in CI, let Dependabot update both files, and retain SHA/policy controls where lockfile coverage has exceptions—especially reusable-workflow dependency boundaries.

practice: Move the v3 tag while keeping or removing the lock entry. Predict the executed commit.
boundary: The model resolves one direct action. It does not run GitHub Actions, generate a real lockfile, cover transitive graphs, reusable-workflow exceptions, policy enforcement, Dependabot, repository compromise, immutable releases, attestations, or vulnerability analysis.

title: gRPC health is scoped to a service name—not every dependency behind it
goal: Publish and consume health status at the same service boundary the client actually calls.
concept:
A mall can be open while one shop is closed. A sign at the parking lot and a sign at the shop answer different questions.

The standard gRPC health service accepts a service name. An empty string can represent the whole server; a named value such as orders.v1.Orders represents that service. Client-side health checking uses the streaming Watch RPC and can stop sending calls when the selected service reports NOT_SERVING. Your application is responsible for updating the status, including shutdown.
example: The process is alive and the catalog service is healthy, but the orders service has lost its database. Server-wide health remains SERVING; orders.v1.Orders must report NOT_SERVING. An orders client watching only the empty name would keep sending doomed calls.

use_case.when: Use standard gRPC health checking when clients or load balancers need a protocol-level signal before routing RPCs.
use_case.example: An EKS gRPC orders service removes only unhealthy orders backends while catalog RPCs on the same process remain available.
use_case.decision: Report the narrowest meaningful service status, wire it to real readiness evidence, update it before shutdown, and test Watch behavior. Keep Kubernetes liveness separate so a downstream outage does not cause pointless process restarts.

practice: Switch the watched name from whole server to orders. Predict whether calls continue during an orders-only database failure.
boundary: The model has one process and two named services. It does not run gRPC, Health.Check/Watch, service config, load balancing, backoff, Kubernetes probes, TLS, database checks, shutdown races, or language-specific implementations.
